We're sharing progress toward understanding the neural activity of language models. We improved methods for training sparse autoencoders at scale, disentangling GPT-4’s internal representations into 16 million features—which often appear to correspond to understandable concepts.
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/ext_tw_video_thumb/1798761957836902402/pu/img/vd_JLIgA4Oc6Mwjl.jpg | https://video.twimg.com/ext_tw_video/1798761957836902402/pu/vid/avc1/480x270/lnRHuPnePZgdeLfp.mp4?tag=14
────────
[2/9] We introduce a new SAE training stack based on a TopK activation function. This eliminates feature shrinking and lets us set L0 directly. We find that our method performs well on the MSE/L0 frontier. Our method has very few dead latents, even at 16M scale.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GPZ_mBLa0AQu0Ve.jpg
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GPZ_mBca0AUCasr.jpg
────────
[3/9] We find clean scaling laws with autoencoder latent count (N) and sparsity (k), as well as with compute (C). We also find that larger subject language models have scaling laws with shallower exponents.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GPaAzWbb0AAuHa2.jpg
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GPaAzVaaQAA4OsC.jpg
────────
[4/9] However, MSE/L0 is not ultimately the thing we care about optimizing. Therefore, we explore several metrics.
- Downstream loss tells us how much of the behavior we're reconstructing, so it upper bounds how much we've explained (but doesn't measure how good the features are)
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GPaD73da0AMv4PO.jpg
────────
[5/9] - Probe loss is an inexpensive metric based on the idea of checking whether the autoencoder recovers features we hypothesize it should have.
- Ablation sparsity is a measure of whether the downstream ablation effects of each latent on the logits is sparse.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GPaFge5aQAAt2X1.jpg

📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GPaGwghbcAARUwZ.jpg

[1/7] Excited to share our latest work on untangling language models by training them with extremely sparse weights! We can isolate tiny circuits inside the model responsible for various simple behaviors and understand them unprecedentedly well.
────────
[2/7] Our circuits are made of literal weight entries that can run in isolation and be directly interpreted. For example, this circuit that closes Python strings uses two MLP neurons and two attention channels total. We can visualize every single weight involved, hiding no detail.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G5qAkhzXUAAug3t.jpg
────────
[3/7] We measure how interpretable our models are by using pruning to isolate the smallest circuit capable of performing each of a suite of simple tasks like the one above. We find much more disentangled circuits in sparse models than in dense models—a >10x difference in circuit size.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G5qAd1QXUAA50EZ.png
────────
[4/7] We find that increasing sparsity (by holding total param count fixed and reducing nonzero param count) moves along the Pareto curve by trading off capability for interpretability, whereas scaling the total model size improves the capability-interpretability Pareto frontier.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G5qAoGHWQAAPSto.jpg
────────
[5/7] We’re excited about scaling up our technique. While it’s unlikely we’ll ever scale to frontier scale, one exciting goal is to train a fully interpretable GPT-3. Such a model organism would teach us important lessons about how AIs work that could transfer to frontier models.
────────
[6/7] We haven’t solved interpretability yet. There is lots of room for improvement, and many of our circuits remain complex. But we can still learn a lot—by inspecting a circuit for closing nested lists, we came up with an adversarial attack that we wouldn’t have thought of otherwise.

summary:
[1/2] the no magic ood principle
a lot of alignment plans have a "magic ood step"; train on data that we can verify, and then hope that it generalizes to the thing we care about, which we can't verify. i think it's worth looking out for these and flagging them! and even if we can't fully avoid it, we should test it via a weak-to-strong type setup, where we actually test several different specific distribution shifts, and try really hard not to contaminate our strong model with human supervision. (this may require, for instance, training the strong model on nothing but weak model generations).
────────
[2/2] a sneaky way to hide a magic ood step that I've seen many times is to define a distribution that has a simple english description, such that it contains the thing we care about as a subset, and then train on data which by definition is a (different) subset of the distribution. this has "iid vibes" and makes it easy to gloss over the part where there is actually a huge ood shift.
